power-of-ten slip in $\Delta v$ or $p$
power-of-ten slip the other way
both the sign error and a tenfold slip

rubric.text: $\Delta v=1/\rho_w-1/\rho_i<0$ because ice is less dense
Multiply by $\Delta p=10^7\ \mathrm{Pa}$ keeping the sign
Check size: tenths of a kelvin

solution:
Clapeyron (phase): $\frac{dT}{dp}=\frac{T\,\Delta v}{L}$ with $\Delta v=v_{water}-v_{ice}$.
$\Delta v=\frac1{1000}-\frac1{917}=-9.05\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{m^3/kg}$ (negative: ice expands on freezing).
$\frac{dT}{dp}=\frac{273(-9.05\times10^{-5})}{3.34\times10^5}=-7.4\times10^{-8}\ \mathrm{K/Pa}$.
$\Delta T=-7.4\times10^{-8}\times10^7=-0.74\ \mathrm K$ (potentials: equal $G$ along the line).
hints: Which phase has the larger specific volume?

prompt: Helium gas ($m=6.64\times10^{-27}\ \mathrm{kg}$ per atom) is at $300\ \mathrm K$ and $1.00\times10^5\ \mathrm{Pa}$. Take $k_B=1.38\times10^{-23}\ \mathrm{J/K}$. Treat the gas as ideal with a Maxwell speed distribution, and count every atom that hits the wall. Find the number of atoms striking a wall per unit area per unit time, in units of $10^{27}\ \mathrm{m^{-2}\,s^{-1}}$.

rubric.text: Mean speed $\bar v=\sqrt{8k_BT/\pi m}$ from the Maxwell distribution
Wall flux is $\tfrac14 n\bar v$ (angular and one-sided average)

solution:
Number density: $n=\frac{p}{k_BT}=2.42\times10^{25}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}}$ (ideal-gas).
Maxwell mean speed: $\bar v=\sqrt{\frac{8k_BT}{\pi m}}=1.26\times10^3\ \mathrm{m/s}$ (kinetic).
Only half the atoms move toward the wall, and the normal component averages to half of that: flux $=\tfrac14n\bar v$.
Flux $=\tfrac14(2.42\times10^{25})(1.26\times10^3)=7.6\times10^{27}\ \mathrm{m^{-2}s^{-1}}$.
hints: Flux is density times mean normal speed, with only one hemisphere of directions.

prompt: A monatomic ideal gas is compressed reversibly and adiabatically to $1/2$ of its volume. By what factor does the number of molecular collisions per unit wall area per unit time change?

why: counted the density increase only and ignored the temperature rise
counted only the speed increase $v_{rms}\propto T^{1/2}$
used the pressure ratio, or $T$ instead of $\sqrt T$ in the flux
used $T$ alone

rubric.text: Flux $\propto n\bar v$ with $n\propto1/V$ and $\bar v\propto\sqrt T$

solution:
Wall collision rate per area $\propto n\bar v$, $\bar v\propto\sqrt T$ (kinetic).
Halving $V$ doubles $n$.
Monatomic adiabat: $TV^{2/3}=$ const, so $T$ rises by $2^{2/3}$ and $\bar v$ by $2^{1/3}$ (gas-processes).
Rate factor $=2\cdot2^{1/3}=2^{4/3}=2.52$.
hints: Rate = density times mean speed, and both change.

prompt: An ideal gas mixture of $2.0\ \mathrm{mol}$ of helium and $1.0\ \mathrm{mol}$ of hydrogen ($\mathrm H_2$, rotation active, vibration frozen) is at $300\ \mathrm K$. It is compressed reversibly and adiabatically until its volume falls by a factor of $8$. Find the final temperature in K.
solution:
Equipartition: He has 3 quadratic terms, $\mathrm H_2$ has 5. $C_V=(3+2.5)R=5.5R$.
Ideal mixture, $n=3$: $C_p=C_V+3R=8.5R$, so $\gamma=1.545$ (equipartition).
Adiabat (gas-processes): $T_fV_f^{\gamma-1}=T_iV_i^{\gamma-1}$.
$T_f=300(8)^{0.5455}=300(3.11)=933\ \mathrm K$.
Trap: using $\gamma=5/3$ gives 1200 K.
hints: Add the heat capacities of the components before forming gamma.

prompt: One mole of ideal gas atoms moves freely on a flat surface in two dimensions with no internal structure. The film has spreading pressure $\varphi$ (force per length) and area $A$, which play the roles of $p$ and $V$, with $\varphi A=Nk_BT$. The work done by the film is $\varphi\,dA$. The film is heated reversibly at constant $\varphi$ by $100\ \mathrm K$. Take $R=8.31\ \mathrm{J/(mol\,K)}$. How much heat does it absorb?

why: used $C_A=R$ (constant area, no work term)
used the three-dimensional $C_V=\tfrac32R$
used the three-dimensional $C_p=\tfrac52R$
used the Dulong-Petit value $3R$

rubric.text: Two quadratic kinetic terms, so $U=Nk_BT=RT$ per mole

solution:
Two translational degrees of freedom: $U=2\cdot\tfrac12RT=RT$ per mole (equipartition).
First law at constant $\varphi$: $Q=\Delta U+\varphi\Delta A$ (first-law).
$\varphi A=RT$ gives $\varphi\Delta A=R\Delta T$.
$C_\varphi=2R$, so $Q=2(8.31)(100)=1662\ \mathrm J$.
hints: Count quadratic terms in two dimensions, then add the work term.

prompt: Four distinguishable oscillators share $6$ identical energy quanta in an isolated system. Every distribution of quanta among the oscillators is equally likely. Find the probability that one particular oscillator holds exactly $3$ quanta.
solution:
Counting quanta in oscillators (stars and bars): $\Omega=\binom{6+4-1}{6}=\binom96=84$ (counting).
Fix oscillator 1 at $3$ quanta. Place $3$ quanta in $3$ oscillators: $\binom{3+3-1}{3}=\binom53=10$.
Equal a priori probability: $P=10/84=0.119$ (entropy: $S=k_B\ln\Omega$).
hints: Count arrangements of quanta with stars and bars.

prompt: A solid contains $N$ independent two-level atoms with energies $0$ and $\varepsilon$. At equilibrium $20\%$ of the atoms are in the upper level, with $N$ very large. What is the entropy per atom in units of $k_B$?

why: used the maximum value $\ln2$, valid only for a $50\%$ population
kept only the up-atom term $-x\ln x$
kept only the down-atom term $-(1-x)\ln(1-x)$
used $\ln5$, treating each atom as one of five choices

solution:
Microstates: $\Omega=\binom{N}{xN}$, $x=0.2$ (counting).
Stirling for large $N$: $\ln\Omega=-N[x\ln x+(1-x)\ln(1-x)]$.
$-0.2\ln0.2=0.322$ and $-0.8\ln0.8=0.178$.
$S/(Nk_B)=0.322+0.178=0.50$, below the maximum $\ln2=0.69$.
hints: Use Stirling's approximation for the binomial coefficient.

prompt: A system has a nondegenerate ground level at energy $0$ and a threefold-degenerate excited level at $\varepsilon=0.050\ \mathrm{eV}$. It is in equilibrium at $500\ \mathrm K$. Take $k_B=1.38\times10^{-23}\ \mathrm{J/K}$ and $q=1.60\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm C$. Find its mean energy in meV.
solution:
$k_BT=\frac{1.38\times10^{-23}(500)}{1.60\times10^{-19}}=0.0431\ \mathrm{eV}$, so $\beta\varepsilon=1.159$.
Degeneracy counts as weight (counting): $Z=1+3e^{-1.159}=1.941$.
$\langle E\rangle=\frac{3\varepsilon e^{-\beta\varepsilon}}{Z}=0.050\cdot\frac{0.941}{1.941}$ (canonical).
$\langle E\rangle=0.0242\ \mathrm{eV}=24.2\ \mathrm{meV}$.
Trap: forgetting the factor $3$ gives $11.9$ meV.
hints: Degenerate levels enter Z with a multiplicity.

prompt: A quantum harmonic oscillator of angular frequency $\omega$ has levels $(n+\tfrac12)\hbar\omega$. At what temperature is its mean total energy equal to $\hbar\omega$?

why: dropped the zero-point energy, so set $\hbar\omega/(e^x-1)=\hbar\omega$
used the classical equipartition value $k_BT=\hbar\omega$
halved the level spacing in the exponent
doubled the level spacing in the exponent

solution:
$Z=\sum e^{-\beta(n+1/2)\hbar\omega}=\frac{e^{-x/2}}{1-e^{-x}}$, $x=\hbar\omega/k_BT$ (canonical).
$\langle E\rangle=-\partial_\beta\ln Z=\hbar\omega\left[\tfrac12+\frac1{e^x-1}\right]$.
Set $\langle E\rangle=\hbar\omega$: $\frac1{e^x-1}=\tfrac12$, so $e^x=3$.
$T=\hbar\omega/(k_B\ln3)=0.91\,\hbar\omega/k_B$.
The classical limit $k_BT=\hbar\omega$ is not reached (equipartition holds only for $k_BT\gg\hbar\omega$).
hints: Include the zero-point term before comparing with hbar omega.

prompt: Conduction electrons in a metal have number density $n=8.5\times10^{28}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}}$. Treat them as a free Fermi gas at $T=0$ with two spin states. Take $\hbar=1.05\times10^{-34}\ \mathrm{J\,s}$, $m_e=9.11\times10^{-31}\ \mathrm{kg}$ and $k_B=1.38\times10^{-23}\ \mathrm{J/K}$. Find the Fermi temperature $E_F/k_B$ in units of $10^4\ \mathrm K$.

rubric.text: Two spin states fill a sphere in $k$-space: $k_F=(3\pi^2n)^{1/3}$

solution:
Free electrons, two spins per $k$ state: $n=\frac{k_F^3}{3\pi^2}$ (quantum-stats).
$k_F=(3\pi^2n)^{1/3}=1.36\times10^{10}\ \mathrm{m^{-1}}$.
$E_F=\frac{\hbar^2k_F^2}{2m_e}=1.12\times10^{-18}\ \mathrm J\approx7.0\ \mathrm{eV}$.
$T_F=E_F/k_B=8.1\times10^4\ \mathrm K$ (kinetic: far above room temperature, so the gas is degenerate).
hints: Count k-space states up to the Fermi sphere including spin.

prompt: Two identical noninteracting particles occupy three degenerate single-particle states. All accessible microstates are equally probable. Let $P_B$ be the probability that both are in the same state for bosons, and $P_D$ the same probability for distinguishable particles. What is $P_B/P_D$?

rubric.text: Distinguishable: $9$ microstates, $3$ with both in one state, $P_D=1/3$

solution:
Distinguishable particles (counting): $3\times3=9$ microstates, $3$ coincident, $P_D=1/3$.
Bosons: unordered pairs. $3$ doubly-occupied states plus $\binom32=3$ states with two different single-particle states $=6$ microstates (quantum-stats).
$P_B=3/6=1/2$.
$P_B/P_D=3/2$, the bunching tendency of bosons. Fermions would give $0$.
hints: Count symmetric two-particle states.

prompt: A star of radius $7.0\times10^{8}\ \mathrm m$ radiates as a blackbody with its spectrum peaking at $500\ \mathrm{nm}$. Use Wien's constant $2.90\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m\,K}$ and $\sigma=5.67\times10^{-8}\ \mathrm{W/(m^2K^4)}$. Find the total radiated power in units of $10^{26}\ \mathrm W$.
solution:
Wien displacement (blackbody): $T=\frac{2.90\times10^{-3}}{5.00\times10^{-7}}=5800\ \mathrm K$.
Surface flux: $\sigma T^4=5.67\times10^{-8}(5800)^4=6.42\times10^{7}\ \mathrm{W/m^2}$ (heat-transfer: radiation).
Area $4\pi R^2=6.16\times10^{18}\ \mathrm{m^2}$.
$P=3.95\times10^{26}\ \mathrm W$.
hints: Peak wavelength fixes temperature, temperature fixes flux.

prompt: Star $B$ has twice the radius of star $A$. Both radiate as blackbodies, and the spectrum of $B$ peaks at half the wavelength of that of $A$. What is the ratio of the total luminosity of $B$ to that of $A$?

Ratio $=(2)^2(2)^4=4\cdot16=64$ (scaling).

prompt: A wall of area $10\ \mathrm{m^2}$ has a brick layer ($k=0.70\ \mathrm{W/(m\,K)}$, thickness $0.20\ \mathrm m$) in series with an insulation layer ($k=0.040\ \mathrm{W/(m\,K)}$, thickness $0.10\ \mathrm m$). The inside surface is at $20\ {}^\circ\mathrm C$ and the outside surface at $-10\ {}^\circ\mathrm C$. Find the steady heat flow through the wall in W.

Same steady heat flow through both layers, like a series circuit (heat-transfer, dc-circuits).
$R_1=\frac{0.20}{0.70(10)}=0.0286\ \mathrm{K/W}$ and $R_2=\frac{0.10}{0.040(10)}=0.250\ \mathrm{K/W}$.
$R_{tot}=0.2786\ \mathrm{K/W}$.
$P=\frac{30}{0.2786}=108\ \mathrm W$.
hints: Treat temperature drop as voltage and heat flow as current.

prompt: A thin flat plate in space faces the Sun with intensity $1360\ \mathrm{W/m^2}$ normal to its front face. The front face absorbs all sunlight. The plate has uniform temperature, and both faces radiate as perfect blackbodies. Use $\sigma=5.67\times10^{-8}\ \mathrm{W/(m^2K^4)}$. What is its equilibrium temperature?

rubric.text: Absorbed power per area is $S$ on the front only
Radiated power per area is $2\sigma T^4$ from two faces

prompt: Which statement is the normalisation condition for $\psi(x)$ in one dimension?

prompt: A particle has $\psi(x)=Ax$ on $0\le x\le 2\ \mathrm m$ and zero elsewhere, with $A>0$ real. Find $A$ in $\mathrm{m^{-3/2}}$ so the state is normalised.
solution: $\int_0^2 A^2x^2\,dx=A^2\cdot\tfrac83=1$, so $A=\sqrt{3/8}\approx0.612$.

prompt: A state is $\psi(x)=A\,e^{-x/a}$ for $x\ge0$ and zero for $x<0$, with $a>0$ and $A>0$. Write $A$ in terms of $a$ so that the state is normalised.

hints: Only the phase carries time dependence in a stationary state.

prompt: A particle of mass $m$ has $E<V_0$ in a region of constant potential $V_0$. Write the decay constant $\kappa$ in $\psi\propto e^{-\kappa x}$ in terms of $\hbar$, $m$, $V_0$ and $E$.
solution: Substituting $e^{-\kappa x}$ gives $\kappa^2\hbar^2/2m=V_0-E$.
hints: Substitute $e^{-\kappa x}$ into the equation.

prompt: State the boundary condition that fixes the energy levels of an infinite square well of width $L$.

why: zero slope at the walls, not zero value
a normalisation mistake: the value at the walls is not 1
a condition at the centre, not at the walls

solution: The wavefunction vanishes at impenetrable walls.
hints: Where is the wavefunction forced to zero?

prompt: For an infinite well, $E_3/E_1$ is a number. Find it.
solution: $E_n\propto n^2$, so $E_3/E_1=9$.
hints: Energies scale as $n^2$.

prompt: How many nodes, meaning zeros strictly inside the well, does the $n=3$ state have?

why: subtracts two from $n$ instead of one
uses $n$ instead of $n-1$
counts the two walls as nodes

solution: The $n$th state has $n-1$ interior zeros.
hints: The walls are not counted as nodes.

prompt: An electron ($m_e=9.11\times10^{-31}\ \mathrm{kg}$, $h=6.63\times10^{-34}\ \mathrm J\,\mathrm s$, $q=1.60\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm C$) is in an infinite well of width $L=1.00\ \mathrm{nm}$. Find $E_3-E_2$ in eV.
solution: $E_n=n^2E_1$ with $E_1=h^2/(8mL^2)\approx0.377$ eV, so $E_3-E_2=5E_1\approx1.88$ eV.
hints: Find $E_1$ first, then use $E_n=n^2E_1$.

prompt: A particle of mass $m$ is in an infinite well of width $L$. Write the gap $E_{n+1}-E_n$ in terms of $\hbar$, $m$, $L$ and $n$.
solution: $E_n=\frac{n^2\pi^2\hbar^2}{2mL^2}$, so $E_{n+1}-E_n=\frac{(2n+1)\pi^2\hbar^2}{2mL^2}$.
hints: Write $E_n=n^2E_1$ and subtract; $(n+1)^2-n^2=2n+1$.

prompt: Normalised eigenfunctions of an infinite well of width $L$ on $0\le x\le L$ are $\psi_n=A\sin(n\pi x/L)$ with $A>0$. Write $A$ in terms of $L$.
solution: $A^2\int_0^L\sin^2(n\pi x/L)\,dx=A^2L/2=1$, so $A=\sqrt{2/L}$.
hints: The integral of $\sin^2$ over one well is $L/2$.

prompt: A particle is in the ground state $\psi_1$ of an infinite well of width $L$. Find the probability of $0\le x\le L/4$ as a decimal.
solution: $\int_0^{L/4}\tfrac2L\sin^2\tfrac{\pi x}{L}\,dx=\tfrac14-\tfrac1{2\pi}\approx0.0908$.
hints: Use $\sin^2\theta=(1-\cos 2\theta)/2$.

prompt: Select all true statements about the ground state of an infinite well.

options: It is nonzero at the centre $x=L/2$
It is zero at both walls

solution: The ground state is positive inside the well and has no interior node. Its energy is $\pi^2\hbar^2/(2mL^2)$, not zero.
hints: Count the zeros of $\sin(\pi x/L)$ strictly inside the well.

prompt: An electron ($m_e=9.11\times10^{-31}\ \mathrm{kg}$, $h=6.63\times10^{-34}\ \mathrm J\,\mathrm s$, $c=3.00\times10^{8}\ \mathrm{m/s}$) falls from $n=2$ to $n=1$ in an infinite well of width $L=0.50\ \mathrm{nm}$. Find the photon wavelength in nm.
solution: $\lambda=hc/(E_2-E_1)$ with $E_2-E_1=3h^2/(8mL^2)$, giving about $275$ nm.
hints: The wavelength is $hc$ divided by the energy gap.

prompt: A particle with energy $E>V_0$ meets a step of height $V_0$. What happens to the wave on the far side?

options: It decays exponentially into the step.
It oscillates with a larger wave number than before.
It oscillates with a smaller wave number, so its wavelength is longer.
It is zero, since the particle cannot enter.
why: that happens only for $E<V_0$
the kinetic energy $E-V_0$ is smaller, so the wave number drops
classically blocked, but a quantum wave partly enters

solution: On the far side the kinetic energy is $E-V_0$, so $k_2<k_1$.
hints: Compare $E-V_0$ with $E$ on the far side.

prompt: A classically forbidden wave decays as $e^{-\kappa x}$ with $\kappa=2.0\ \mathrm{nm^{-1}}$. Find the distance in nm over which the probability density falls by a factor $e$.
solution: $|\psi|^2\propto e^{-2\kappa x}$, so the distance is $1/(2\kappa)=0.25$ nm.
hints: Density depends on $\psi$ squared.

prompt: For a barrier with $E<V_0$, which statement about the transmission probability $T$ is correct?

options: $T$ is small but nonzero, and it falls exponentially with barrier width.
$T$ is independent of the barrier width.
why: the classical result; quantum tunnelling gives $T>0$
width enters through $e^{-2\kappa a}$
a classical-looking ratio, not the quantum result

solution: Tunnelling is exponentially sensitive to barrier width.
hints: What does the decaying wave do across a thick barrier?

prompt: An electron ($\hbar=1.05\times10^{-34}$ J s, $m_e=9.11\times10^{-31}$ kg, $q=1.60\times10^{-19}$ C) has $E=1.0$ eV and meets a barrier of height $V_0=5.0$ eV and width $a=0.20$ nm. Using the WKB estimate $T\approx e^{-2\kappa a}$ with $\kappa=\sqrt{2m(V_0-E)}/\hbar$, find $T$.
solution: $\kappa\approx1.03\times10^{10}\ \mathrm{m^{-1}}$, so $2\kappa a\approx4.11$ and $T\approx0.0163$.
hints: Compute $\kappa$ first, then $2\kappa a$.

prompt: A particle with energy $E=2V_0$ meets a sharp step of height $V_0$ from the left. Find the reflection probability as a decimal, using the exact step result.
solution: $R=\left(\frac{k_1-k_2}{k_1+k_2}\right)^2$ with $k_2/k_1=1/\sqrt2$, so $R=(\sqrt2-1)^4\approx0.0294$.
hints: The ratio $k_2/k_1=\sqrt{(E-V_0)/E}$.

prompt: A particle with $E>V_0$ sits on the far side of a step of height $V_0$. Write its wave number $k_2$ there in terms of $\hbar$, $m$, $E$ and $V_0$.
solution: Kinetic energy on the far side is $E-V_0$, so $k_2=\sqrt{2m(E-V_0)}/\hbar$.
hints: Only the kinetic energy $E-V_0$ enters the wave number.

prompt: A barrier has $\kappa=1.5\ \mathrm{nm^{-1}}$. Using $T\approx e^{-2\kappa a}$, find the ratio $T(a=2.0\ \mathrm{nm})/T(a=1.0\ \mathrm{nm})$ as a decimal.
solution: The ratio is $e^{-2\kappa(2-1)}=e^{-3}\approx0.0498$.
hints: Only the difference in width matters in the ratio.

prompt: Select all true statements about tunnelling through a thick barrier with $E<V_0$.

options: $T$ grows as the barrier gets thicker
$T$ grows as $E$ rises towards $V_0$ from below

solution: Transmission falls as $e^{-2\kappa a}$. Since $\kappa$ shrinks as $E\to V_0$, $T$ grows.
hints: Look at how $\kappa$ depends on $E$ and $a$.

prompt: An electron with $E=1.0$ eV meets a barrier of height $V_0=3.0$ eV. Using WKB, $T\approx e^{-2\kappa a}$, find the barrier width $a$ in nm at which $T=10^{-3}$. Use $\hbar=1.05\times10^{-34}$ J s, $m_e=9.11\times10^{-31}$ kg and $q=1.60\times10^{-19}$ C.
solution: $\kappa\approx7.27\ \mathrm{nm^{-1}}$ for $V_0-E=2.0$ eV, so $a=\ln(1000)/(2\kappa)\approx0.475$ nm.
hints: Invert $T=e^{-2\kappa a}$ for $a$.

prompt: State the energy levels of a one-dimensional harmonic oscillator with angular frequency $\omega$.

why: drops the zero-point energy
wrong offset: the ground state is $\hbar\omega/2$
quadratic spacing belongs to the infinite well

solution: The oscillator levels are evenly spaced with a half-quantum zero-point energy.
hints: What is the ground-state energy?

prompt: Find the ground-state energy of the harmonic oscillator in units of $\hbar\omega$.
solution: $E_0=\tfrac12\hbar\omega$.
hints: The zero-point term is half a quantum.

prompt: What is the spacing between adjacent levels of the harmonic oscillator?

why: that is the zero-point energy, not the spacing
counts two steps per quantum
wrong dimensions: an energy needs $\hbar\omega$

solution: Adjacent levels differ by one quantum $\hbar\omega$.
hints: Subtract $E_n$ from $E_{n+1}$.

prompt: A harmonic oscillator has $\hbar\omega=2.0$ eV. Find the energy of the $n=2$ level in eV.
solution: $E_2=(2+\tfrac12)\hbar\omega=5.0$ eV.
hints: The zero-point term is $\tfrac12\hbar\omega$.

prompt: An electron ($m_e=9.11\times10^{-31}$ kg) is in the ground state of an oscillator with $\hbar\omega=0.10$ eV. Use $\hbar=1.05\times10^{-34}$ J s and $q=1.60\times10^{-19}$ C. Find the rms displacement $\sqrt{\langle x^2\rangle}$ in nm.
solution: $\langle x^2\rangle=\hbar/(2m\omega)=\hbar^2/(2m\,\hbar\omega)\approx3.78\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm m^2$, so rms $\approx0.615$ nm.
hints: Write $\omega=\hbar\omega/\hbar$ before substituting.

prompt: A particle of mass $m$ sits in the potential $V=\tfrac12kx^2$ with spring constant $k$. Write the energy $E_n$ of level $n$ in terms of $\hbar$, $k$, $m$ and $n$.
solution: $\omega=\sqrt{k/m}$ from $k=m\omega^2$, so $E_n=(n+\tfrac12)\hbar\sqrt{k/m}$.
hints: Match $\tfrac12kx^2$ to $\tfrac12m\omega^2x^2$ first.

prompt: The ground state of an oscillator with mass $m$ and frequency $\omega$ is $\psi_0=A\exp(-m\omega x^2/2\hbar)$ with $A>0$. Write $A$ in terms of $m$, $\omega$ and $\hbar$.
solution: $A^2\int e^{-m\omega x^2/\hbar}\,dx=A^2\sqrt{\pi\hbar/(m\omega)}=1$, so $A=(m\omega/\pi\hbar)^{1/4}$.
hints: Use $\int e^{-\alpha x^2}dx=\sqrt{\pi/\alpha}$ with $\alpha=m\omega/\hbar$.

prompt: Select all true statements about the one-dimensional harmonic oscillator.

options: Parity alternates from one level to the next
The ground-state wavefunction has a node at $x=0$

solution: Spacing is $\hbar\omega$, the zero-point energy is $\hbar\omega/2$, and parity alternates. The ground state is a single Gaussian with no node.
hints: The ground state is a Gaussian.

prompt: An oscillator has $\hbar\omega=0.40$ eV. Find the lowest photon energy in eV that can drive a dipole-allowed transition out of the ground state.
solution: Dipole transitions change $n$ by one, so $n=0\to1$ needs $\hbar\omega$. The $0\to2$ jump is forbidden.
hints: Which change in $n$ does a dipole transition allow?

prompt: State the canonical commutator of position $x$ and momentum $p$ in one dimension.

why: they do not commute
missing the factor $i$
sign reversed; this is $[p,x]$

solution: Position and momentum satisfy $[x,p]=i\hbar$.
hints: Which order gives the positive sign?

prompt: Write $[x,p^3]=c\,i\hbar\,p^2$. Find $c$.
hints: Use $[x,p^n]=i\hbar\,n\,p^{n-1}$.

prompt: Which property guarantees that an observable has real eigenvalues?

options: The operator has no zero eigenvalue.
why: unitary eigenvalues have modulus 1, not necessarily real
commutation does not make eigenvalues real
a nonzero spectrum says nothing about reality

solution: Hermitian operators have real eigenvalues.
hints: Which condition is $A^\dagger=A$?

prompt: Compute $[x^2,p]=c\,i\hbar\,x$. Find $c$.
solution: $[x^2,p]=x[x,p]+[x,p]x=2i\hbar x$, so $c=2$.
hints: Use $[AB,C]=A[B,C]+[A,C]B$ with $[x,p]=i\hbar$.

prompt: A particle of mass $m$ has $H=p^2/2m+Fx$ with constant $F$. Using Ehrenfest's theorem, write $d^2\langle x\rangle/dt^2$ in terms of $F$ and $m$.
solution: $d\langle x\rangle/dt=\langle p\rangle/m$ and $d\langle p\rangle/dt=-\langle dV/dx\rangle=-F$, so $d^2\langle x\rangle/dt^2=-F/m$.
hints: Apply $d\langle A\rangle/dt=\tfrac{i}{\hbar}\langle[H,A]\rangle$ twice.

prompt: In an orthonormal basis $\{|1\rangle,|2\rangle\}$, a Hermitian operator has matrix $\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}$. Find its largest eigenvalue.
solution: Eigenvalues are $2\pm1$, so the largest is $3$.
hints: Solve $\det(A-\lambda I)=0$.

prompt: A Hermitian operator $A$ has $A|1\rangle=|1\rangle$ and $A|2\rangle=3|2\rangle$ in an orthonormal basis. The state is $|\psi\rangle=(|1\rangle+|2\rangle)/\sqrt2$. Find $\langle A\rangle$.
solution: $\langle A\rangle=\tfrac12\cdot1+\tfrac12\cdot3=2$.
hints: Expectation is the weighted average of eigenvalues by probability.

prompt: Select all operators that are Hermitian.
solution: $x$ and $p$ are Hermitian. $ix$ is anti-Hermitian, and $xp$ is not Hermitian because $(xp)^\dagger=px$.
hints: Check $A^\dagger=A$ for each operator.

prompt: Let $O=x^2p$. Write $[O,x]=c\,i\hbar\,x^2$. Find $c$.
hints: Only $p$ fails to commute with $x$.

prompt: State the position-momentum uncertainty relation.

why: factor 2 wrong: the bound is $\hbar/2$
a sum, not a product
units wrong: $\Delta x\,\Delta p$ has units of $\hbar$

solution: The product of spreads is bounded by $\hbar/2$.
hints: Check both the factor and the units.

prompt: In units of $\hbar$, what is the minimum value of $\Delta x\,\Delta p$ for any state?
solution: The minimum is $\hbar/2$, reached by Gaussian packets.
hints: Gaussian packets saturate the bound.

prompt: Which pair of observables can be measured simultaneously with no uncertainty bound?

why: non-commuting, so a bound applies
non-commuting: $[L_x,L_y]=i\hbar L_z$

solution: Commuting observables have no uncertainty bound.
hints: Which pairs have zero commutator?

prompt: A particle is localised to $\Delta x=0.10$ nm. Find the minimum $\Delta p$ in units of $\hbar/\mathrm{nm}$.
solution: $\Delta p_{\min}=\hbar/(2\Delta x)=5.0\,\hbar/\mathrm{nm}$.
hints: Use the equality case of the bound.

prompt: An electron ($m_e=9.11\times10^{-31}$ kg, $\hbar=1.05\times10^{-34}$ J s, $q=1.60\times10^{-19}$ C) is confined to $\Delta x=0.20$ nm. Take $\langle p^2\rangle=(\Delta p)^2$ at the minimum and find the minimum kinetic energy in eV.
solution: $\Delta p=\hbar/(2\Delta x)$, so $K=(\Delta p)^2/2m=\hbar^2/(8m\Delta x^2)\approx0.236$ eV.
hints: Substitute the minimum $\Delta p$ into $p^2/2m$.

prompt: A Gaussian packet has minimum spread $\Delta x=a$. Write its minimum $\Delta p$ in terms of $\hbar$ and $a$.
solution: $\Delta p_{\min}=\hbar/(2a)$.
hints: Use $\Delta x\,\Delta p=\hbar/2$ as an equality.

prompt: A state has energy spread set by a lifetime $\Delta t=1.0$ ns. Using $\Delta E\,\Delta t\ge\hbar/2$ with $\hbar=1.05\times10^{-34}$ J s and $q=1.60\times10^{-19}$ C, find the minimum $\Delta E$ in $\mu$eV.
solution: $\Delta E_{\min}=\hbar/(2\Delta t)\approx3.28\times10^{-7}$ eV, which is $0.328\ \mu$eV.
hints: Convert joules to eV before converting to $\mu$eV.

prompt: Select all pairs whose commutator is nonzero, so that $\sigma_A\sigma_B\ge\tfrac12|\langle[A,B]\rangle|$ can give a bound.
solution: $[x,p_x]=i\hbar$ and $[L_x,L_y]=i\hbar L_z$ give bounds. Position components commute, and $L_z$ commutes with $L^2$.
hints: A bound exists only when the commutator is nonzero.

prompt: By what factor does the minimum $\Delta p$ change when $\Delta x$ is halved?
solution: $\Delta p_{\min}\propto1/\Delta x$, so halving $\Delta x$ doubles $\Delta p_{\min}$.
hints: Minimum $\Delta p$ is inversely proportional to $\Delta x$.

prompt: Write the expectation value $\langle A\rangle$ of observable $A$ in a normalised state $|\psi\rangle$.

why: scales $A$ by the norm; that is a number, not an expectation
$A$ is not a bra
squares the amplitude instead of sandwiching $A$

solution: The expectation value sandwiches $A$ between the state and its bra.
hints: Where does the operator $A$ sit in the bracket?

prompt: Let $|\psi\rangle=|1\rangle+2|2\rangle$ in an orthonormal basis. Find $\langle\psi|\psi\rangle$.
solution: $\langle\psi|\psi\rangle=1^2+2^2=5$.
hints: Sum the squared components.

prompt: Which expression is the completeness relation for an orthonormal basis $\{|n\rangle\}$?

why: counts the basis states, giving the dimension
kets cannot be summed to a number
amplitudes must be squared for probabilities

solution: The projectors onto basis states sum to the identity.
hints: Sum projectors, not kets or numbers.

prompt: A normalised state is $|\psi\rangle=0.6|1\rangle+0.8|2\rangle$ in an orthonormal basis. Find the probability of measuring $|2\rangle$, as a fraction.
hints: Probability is the squared amplitude.

prompt: For the state $0.6|1\rangle+0.8|2\rangle$, the observable $A$ has eigenvalue $2$ on $|1\rangle$ and $-1$ on $|2\rangle$. Find $\langle A\rangle$ as a fraction.
solution: $\langle A\rangle=0.36\cdot2-0.64=0.08=\tfrac{2}{25}$.
hints: Weight each eigenvalue by its probability.

prompt: A normalised state $N(|1\rangle+k|2\rangle)$ has real $k$. Write the prefactor $N>0$ in terms of $k$.
hints: Set the sum of squared amplitudes to 1.

prompt: In an orthonormal basis, $A|1\rangle=5|1\rangle+3|2\rangle$ and $A|2\rangle=|2\rangle$. Find the matrix element $\langle 2|A|1\rangle$.
solution: $\langle 2|A|1\rangle$ is the $|2\rangle$ component of $A|1\rangle$, which is $3$.
hints: Read off the $|2\rangle$ coefficient of $A|1\rangle$.

prompt: Select all true statements about an orthonormal basis $\{|n\rangle\}$.
solution: Orthonormality gives the Kronecker delta. $|\psi\rangle\langle\psi|$ is an operator, and $\langle\psi|\phi\rangle$ is the conjugate of $\langle\phi|\psi\rangle$.
hints: Check each statement against the conjugate symmetry of the inner product.

prompt: For the state $0.6|1\rangle+0.8|2\rangle$, find $\langle\sigma_x\rangle$ where $\sigma_x=|1\rangle\langle2|+|2\rangle\langle1|$. Give the answer as a fraction.
solution: $\langle\sigma_x\rangle=2\cdot0.6\cdot0.8=\tfrac{24}{25}$.
hints: The sandwich picks out the two cross terms.

prompt: What are the possible results of measuring $S_z$ for a spin-one-half particle?

why: wrong scale: spin one-half gives $\pm\hbar/2$
dimensionless: forgets $\hbar$
spin-one values

solution: Spin one-half gives two outcomes, each $\pm\hbar/2$.
hints: What is the scale of the spin?

prompt: For a spin-up state along $z$, find $\langle\sigma_z\rangle$.
solution: $\langle\sigma_z\rangle=+1$ for spin up.
hints: Pauli $\sigma_z$ has eigenvalues $\pm1$.

prompt: Which commutator is correct for spin components?

why: missing the factor $i$
spin components do not commute
wrong component on the right

solution: Spin components satisfy the cyclic angular momentum algebra.
hints: Use the cyclic pattern $xyz$.

prompt: A spin-one-half particle is prepared in $|{+}\rangle_z$, spin up along $z$. Find the probability that a measurement of $S_x$ gives $+\hbar/2$, as a fraction.
solution: $|{+}\rangle_z=(|{+}\rangle_x+|{-}\rangle_x)/\sqrt2$, so $P=\tfrac12$.
hints: Write $|{+}\rangle_z$ in the $x$ basis.

prompt: A spin-one-half state is $\cos(\theta/2)|{+}\rangle+\sin(\theta/2)|{-}\rangle$ in the $z$ basis. Write $\langle\sigma_z\rangle$ as a function of $\theta$.
solution: $\langle\sigma_z\rangle=\cos^2(\theta/2)-\sin^2(\theta/2)=\cos\theta$.
hints: Use the double-angle identity for cosine.

prompt: A spin-one-half state is $\tfrac{1}{\sqrt5}(2|{+}\rangle+|{-}\rangle)$ in the $z$ basis. Find the probability of $S_z=-\hbar/2$, as a fraction.
solution: The $|{-}\rangle$ amplitude is $1/\sqrt5$, so $P=\tfrac15$.
hints: Square the amplitude of $|{-}\rangle$.

prompt: A spin-one-half Hamiltonian is $H=\beta\sigma_z$ with $\beta=0.40$ eV. Find the lower energy eigenvalue in eV.
solution: Eigenvalues are $\pm\beta$. The lower one is $-0.40$ eV.
hints: Diagonalise $\sigma_z$ first.

prompt: Select all true statements about a single spin-one-half particle.

options: The spin states form a three-dimensional space

solution: Pauli matrices square to the identity. $\sigma_x$ and $\sigma_z$ anticommute, and spin one-half lives in two dimensions.
hints: A spin one-half space has two orthogonal states.

prompt: A spin-one-half state is $\cos\alpha\,|{+}\rangle+\sin\alpha\,|{-}\rangle$ with real $\alpha$. Write $\langle\sigma_x\rangle$ as a function of $\alpha$.
solution: $\langle\sigma_x\rangle=2\cos\alpha\sin\alpha=\sin2\alpha$.
hints: The off-diagonal term of $\sigma_x$ gives $2ab$.

prompt: For orbital angular momentum $\ell=2$, which values can $L_z$ take?

why: misses the negative $m$ values
the $\ell=1$ set
$L_z$ is not fixed by $\ell$ alone

solution: For each $\ell$, $m$ runs from $-\ell$ to $\ell$.
hints: Include both signs of $m$.

prompt: For $\ell=1$, find $|\mathbf L|$ in units of $\hbar$.
solution: $|\mathbf L|=\sqrt{\ell(\ell+1)}\,\hbar=\sqrt2\,\hbar$.
hints: Use $\mathbf L^2=\ell(\ell+1)\hbar^2$.

prompt: How many $m$ states belong to a multiplet with orbital quantum number $\ell$?

why: counts only $m\ge0$
misses $m=0$
a square, not a count

solution: $m$ runs over $2\ell+1$ integers.
hints: Count from $-\ell$ to $\ell$ inclusive.

prompt: For $\ell=3$, find $|\mathbf L|$ in units of $\hbar$.
solution: $|\mathbf L|=\sqrt{\ell(\ell+1)}\,\hbar=\sqrt{12}\,\hbar\approx3.46\,\hbar$.
hints: Use $\sqrt{\ell(\ell+1)}$.

prompt: For $\ell=1$ and $m=1$, find the angle in degrees between $\mathbf L$ and the $z$ axis.
solution: $\cos\theta=L_z/|\mathbf L|=1/\sqrt2$, so $\theta=45^\circ$.
hints: Take $\cos\theta=L_z/|\mathbf L|$.

prompt: For the state $|\ell,m\rangle$ write the eigenvalue of $L_x^2+L_y^2$ in terms of $\hbar$, $\ell$ and $m$.
solution: $L_x^2+L_y^2=\mathbf L^2-L_z^2$, so the eigenvalue is $\hbar^2[\ell(\ell+1)-m^2]$.
hints: Subtract $L_z^2$ from $\mathbf L^2$.

prompt: $L_+|\ell{=}2,m{=}1\rangle=c\,\hbar\,|2,2\rangle$. Find $c$.
hints: Use $L_+$ with $\sqrt{\ell(\ell+1)-m(m+1)}$.

prompt: Select all true statements about $\ell=1$.
solution: $L_z\in\{-\hbar,0,\hbar\}$ and $|\mathbf L|=\sqrt2\hbar$. $L_z$ is never $\pm\sqrt2\hbar$, and $\mathbf L$ never points exactly along $z$.
hints: $L_z$ takes values $m\hbar$ with $m$ an integer.

prompt: $L_-|\ell{=}2,m{=}0\rangle=c\,\hbar\,|2,-1\rangle$. Find $c$ in units of $\hbar$ as a decimal.
solution: $c=\sqrt{\ell(\ell+1)-m(m-1)}=\sqrt{6}\approx2.449$.
hints: Use $L_-$ with $\sqrt{\ell(\ell+1)-m(m-1)}$.

prompt: For a time-independent Hamiltonian $H$, which operator gives $|\psi(t)\rangle=U(t)|\psi(0)\rangle$?

why: drops the factor $i$, giving imaginary-time decay
drops $\hbar$ from the exponent
wrong sign: this evolves backwards in time

solution: Time evolution is unitary, $U=e^{-iHt/\hbar}$.
hints: What is the sign and the $i$ in the exponent?

prompt: A superposition of two energy eigenstates has $E_2-E_1=3\hbar\omega$. Its expectation values oscillate at angular frequency $\Omega$. In units of $\omega$, find $\Omega$.
solution: $\Omega=(E_2-E_1)/\hbar=3\omega$.
hints: Divide the energy gap by $\hbar$.

prompt: A state is a superposition of two energy eigenstates. Which statement about its probability density $|\psi(x,t)|^2$ is correct?

why: true only for a single stationary state
adds the energies instead of subtracting
ignores the phase of the lower state

solution: Interference between the two components gives an oscillation at the energy gap over $\hbar$.
hints: Which energy difference appears in the cross term?

prompt: A two-level superposition has energy gap $\Delta E=4.0$ eV. Use $h=6.63\times10^{-34}$ J s and $q=1.60\times10^{-19}$ C. Find its period in fs.
solution: Period $T=h/\Delta E\approx1.04$ fs.
hints: Period is $h$ over the energy gap.

prompt: An energy eigenstate with $E=2.0$ eV evolves for $t=1.0$ fs. Use $\hbar=1.05\times10^{-34}$ J s and $q=1.60\times10^{-19}$ C. Find the phase $Et/\hbar$ in radians.
solution: $Et/\hbar=3.2\times10^{-34}/1.05\times10^{-34}\approx3.05$ rad.
hints: Convert eV to joules first.

prompt: A superposition of the $n=1$ and $n=2$ levels of an infinite well of width $L$ and mass $m$ oscillates in time. Write its angular frequency $\Omega$ in terms of $\hbar$, $m$ and $L$.
hints: Beat frequency is the energy gap over $\hbar$.

prompt: Two levels in a superposition are split by $1.0$ meV. Use $h=6.63\times10^{-34}$ J s and $q=1.60\times10^{-19}$ C. Find the period in ps of the superposition, $t=h/\Delta E$.
solution: $t=h/\Delta E=6.63\times10^{-34}/1.6\times10^{-22}\approx4.14$ ps.
hints: Convert meV to joules.

prompt: Select all true statements about an energy eigenstate $\psi_n(x)e^{-iE_nt/\hbar}$.
solution: The phase rotates at $E_n/\hbar$ and $|\psi|^2$ is fixed. The energy is sharp, so $\langle H\rangle=E_n$ is constant.
hints: Only the phase carries time dependence.

prompt: A superposition of the oscillator levels $n=0$ and $n=2$ has energies $\tfrac12\hbar\omega$ and $\tfrac52\hbar\omega$. Its beat angular frequency is $\Omega$. In units of $\omega$, find $\Omega$.
solution: $\Omega=(\tfrac52-\tfrac12)\omega=2\omega$.
hints: Subtract the two energies and divide by $\hbar$.

prompt: After a projective measurement of $S_z$ gives $+\hbar/2$, what is the state?

options: The original state, since measurements do not disturb the system.
why: the outcome was $+$, so the state is not $-$
the pre-measurement superposition; collapse removes the $-$ part
projective measurement collapses the state onto the outcome

solution: A projective measurement collapses the state onto the eigenstate of the outcome.
hints: Which eigenstate matches the outcome?

prompt: For $H=\tfrac12\hbar\Omega\sigma_x$ starting in $|{\uparrow}\rangle$, find the maximum probability of $|{\downarrow}\rangle$ over all times.
solution: $P_\downarrow=\sin^2(\Omega t/2)$ reaches 1 at $\Omega t=\pi$.
hints: The flip probability is a squared sine.

prompt: For $H=\tfrac12\hbar\Omega\sigma_x$, what are the energy eigenvalues?

why: twice the correct magnitude
a shifted pair, not symmetric about zero
drops $\hbar$ from the energy

solution: $\sigma_x$ has eigenvalues $\pm1$, so $H$ has $\pm\hbar\Omega/2$.
hints: What are the eigenvalues of $\sigma_x$?

prompt: Starting in $|{\uparrow}\rangle$ with $H=\tfrac12\hbar\Omega\sigma_x$, find the probability of $|{\downarrow}\rangle$ at $t=\pi/(4\Omega)$ as a decimal.
solution: $P_\downarrow=\sin^2(\Omega t/2)=\sin^2(\pi/8)\approx0.1464$.
hints: Evaluate $\Omega t/2$ first.

prompt: With $H=\tfrac12\hbar\Omega\sigma_x$ and $\Omega=2.0\times10^{12}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$, find the time in ps for the first complete flip from $|{\uparrow}\rangle$ to $|{\downarrow}\rangle$.
solution: $P_\downarrow=\sin^2(\Omega t/2)$ reaches 1 at $\Omega t=\pi$, so $t=\pi/\Omega\approx1.571$ ps.
hints: Find the time where $\Omega t/2=\pi/2$.

prompt: With $H=\tfrac12\hbar\Omega\sigma_x$ and initial state $|{\uparrow}\rangle$, write the probability of $|{\downarrow}\rangle$ at time $t$ in terms of $\Omega$ and $t$.
solution: $P_\downarrow=\sin^2(\Omega t/2)=\tfrac12(1-\cos\Omega t)$.
hints: Use $\sin^2 x=\tfrac12(1-\cos2x)$.

prompt: A spin is prepared in $S_x=+\hbar/2$. A $S_z$ measurement gives $+\hbar/2$, and then an $S_x$ measurement is made. Find the joint probability that both outcomes are $+\hbar/2$, as a fraction.
solution: $P(+z)=\tfrac12$. The collapsed state $|{+}z\rangle$ gives $P(+x)=\tfrac12$, so the joint probability is $\tfrac14$.
hints: Use the post-measurement state for the second step.

prompt: Select all true statements about a projective measurement of $\sigma_z$ on $a|{\uparrow}\rangle+b|{\downarrow}\rangle$, with $|a|^2+|b|^2=1$.

options: Repeating the measurement at once gives the same outcome
Both outcomes have probability $\tfrac12$ for any $a$, $b$

solution: Born's rule gives $|a|^2$. Collapse gives $|{\uparrow}\rangle$, and an immediate repeat gives the same outcome. Equal probabilities hold only for special $a$, $b$.
hints: Apply Born's rule and then collapse.

prompt: With $H=\tfrac12\hbar\Omega\sigma_x$ and initial state $|{\uparrow}\rangle$, write the first time $t>0$ at which $P_\downarrow=1$ in terms of $\Omega$.
solution: $\sin^2(\Omega t/2)=1$ first at $\Omega t/2=\pi/2$, so $t=\pi/\Omega$.
hints: Set $\Omega t/2=\pi/2$.

prompt: What is the first-order energy correction for a nondegenerate level $|n\rangle$ under perturbation $H'$?

why: the unperturbed energy, not a correction
off-diagonal elements do not shift the level at first order
squares the expectation instead of taking it

solution: The first-order shift is the diagonal expectation of $H'$.
hints: Which matrix element is diagonal?

prompt: State the sign of the second-order energy shift of the ground state, as $+1$ or $-1$.
solution: Ground-state second-order shifts are negative, since every term has $E_1-E_m<0$.
hints: Second-order sums have denominators $E_n-E_m$.

prompt: When is first-order perturbation theory reliable?

options: When the perturbation matrix elements are small compared with the level spacings.
Only when the unperturbed states are plane waves.
why: perturbation theory needs $H'$ small
degenerate levels need a different treatment
any complete set of unperturbed states works

solution: The expansion needs small corrections relative to the spacings.
hints: What must be small?

prompt: An infinite well of width $L$ has ground state $\psi_1$. A perturbation $H'=V_0$ acts only for $L/2<x<L$, with $V_0=0.80$ eV. Using first-order perturbation theory, find the shift of the ground-state energy in eV.
hints: Integrate $|\psi_1|^2$ over the right half of the well.

prompt: An infinite well of width $L=1.0$ nm on $0<x<L$ has ground state $\psi_1$. A perturbation $H'=\lambda x^2$ with $\lambda=1.0$ eV/nm$^2$ acts on the well. Using first-order perturbation theory, find the ground-state shift in eV.
solution: $\langle x^2\rangle_1=L^2\left(\tfrac13-\tfrac{1}{2\pi^2}\right)\approx0.283L^2$, so $E^{(1)}\approx0.283$ eV.
hints: Use $\langle x^2\rangle_n=L^2\left(\tfrac13-\tfrac{1}{2n^2\pi^2}\right)$.

prompt: An infinite well of width $L$ has perturbation $H'=\lambda x$ with constant $\lambda$. Using first-order perturbation theory on the ground state $\psi_1$, write the energy shift in terms of $\lambda$ and $L$.
solution: $\langle1|x|1\rangle=L/2$, since $|\psi_1|^2$ is symmetric about the centre.
hints: Where is the centre of $|\psi_1|^2$?

prompt: A degenerate two-level subspace has a perturbation $H'$ with matrix $\begin{pmatrix}0&0.20\\0.20&0\end{pmatrix}$ eV in that subspace. Using degenerate perturbation theory, find the energy splitting in eV.
solution: Diagonalising inside the subspace gives $\pm0.20$ eV, which split by $0.40$ eV.
hints: Diagonalise the matrix inside the degenerate subspace.

prompt: Select all true statements about first-order perturbation theory.

options: It requires $H'$ to be small compared with level spacings
It gives the exact energy for any strength of $H'$
The ground-state second-order shift is always positive

solution: First-order shifts are diagonal expectations, valid for small $H'$. The method is approximate, and second-order shifts of ground states are negative.
hints: Check which statements depend on $H'$ being small.

prompt: Two unperturbed levels are $E_1=0$ and $E_2=1.0$ eV. A perturbation couples them with $\langle1|H'|2\rangle=0.10$ eV and has no diagonal terms. Using second-order perturbation theory, find the shift of $E_1$ in eV.
hints: Second-order shift is $|V|^2$ over the energy difference.

prompt: For a trial state $|\psi\rangle$, which statement is the variational principle?

options: $\langle H\rangle_\psi\le E_0$ for every trial state.
$\langle H\rangle_\psi\ge E_0$ for every trial state.
$\langle H\rangle_\psi\ge E_1$ for every trial state.
why: reverses the inequality
equality holds only for the exact ground state
the bound is on $E_0$, not on $E_1$

solution: Every trial energy lies above the ground-state energy.
hints: Which direction is the bound?

prompt: The WKB condition $\oint p\,dx=(n+\gamma)h$ has Maslov phase $\gamma$. Find $\gamma$ for a smooth well with two turning points.
solution: Two turning points give $\gamma=\tfrac12$.
hints: Each turning point contributes a quarter cycle.

prompt: When is the WKB approximation accurate?

options: When the potential varies slowly compared with the local wavelength.
When the energy is much smaller than the potential everywhere.
why: WKB fails at turning points; they need a connection formula
ignores the oscillating region needed for quantisation
WKB applies to all levels in the semiclassical regime

solution: WKB needs slow variation on the scale of the wavelength.
hints: What does 'slowly varying' mean for the wave?

prompt: Use the variational (Rayleigh-ratio) method with the unnormalised trial function $\psi=x(L-x)$ on $0\le x\le L$ and $H=-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\frac{d^2}{dx^2}$. Find the upper bound on $E_0$ in units of $\hbar^2/(2mL^2)$.
solution: $\langle H\rangle=\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\frac{\int\psi'^2}{\int\psi^2}=\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\cdot\frac{10}{L^2}$. Exact $E_0$ is $\pi^2\approx9.87$.
hints: Use $\int\psi'^2dx=L^3/3$ and $\int\psi^2dx=L^5/30$.

prompt: Using the WKB estimate $T\approx e^{-2\int\kappa\,dx}$ with $\int\kappa\,dx=2.0$, find $T$ as a decimal.
solution: $T\approx e^{-4}\approx0.0183$.
hints: Double the exponent first.

prompt: Use the trial function $\psi=\exp(-\alpha x^2)$ with $\alpha>0$ for $H=p^2/2m+\tfrac12m\omega^2x^2$. Write $\langle H\rangle=\int\psi H\psi\,dx/\int\psi^2dx$ as a function of $\alpha$.
solution: $\langle p^2\rangle=\hbar^2\alpha$ and $\langle x^2\rangle=1/(4\alpha)$, so $\langle H\rangle=\hbar^2\alpha/2m+m\omega^2/8\alpha$.
hints: Find $\langle p^2\rangle$ and $\langle x^2\rangle$ for the Gaussian.

prompt: Use the trial function $\psi=\exp(-\alpha x^2)$ for $H=p^2/2m+\tfrac12m\omega^2x^2$. Minimise $\langle H\rangle$ over $\alpha>0$ and give the lowest value in units of $\hbar\omega$.
solution: The minimum is at $\alpha=m\omega/2\hbar$, giving $\langle H\rangle=\tfrac12\hbar\omega$.
hints: Set the derivative with respect to $\alpha$ to zero.

prompt: Select all true statements about the variational and WKB methods.

options: The variational method gives an upper bound on the ground-state energy
WKB is accurate when the potential varies slowly on the scale of the local wavelength
WKB gives exact energies for every potential
The variational method gives a lower bound on the ground-state energy

solution: Variational energies sit above $E_0$. WKB is good for slowly varying potentials, and it is approximate.
hints: Think about which direction the variational bound points.

prompt: A WKB well obeys $\int p\,dx=(n+\tfrac12)\pi\hbar$. For $n=3$, find $\int p\,dx$ in units of $\pi\hbar$.
solution: $\int p\,dx=(3+\tfrac12)\pi\hbar=\tfrac72\pi\hbar$.
hints: Add one half to $n$.

prompt: Which statement about identical fermions is correct?

options: The total wavefunction is symmetric under exchange.
The spatial wavefunction is always antisymmetric.
They can occupy the same complete state.
The total wavefunction is antisymmetric under exchange.

antisymmetry applies to the total state, and spin can carry it
Pauli exclusion forbids this

hints: Which symmetry applies to fermions?

prompt: How many spin-one-half fermions at most can occupy one spatial orbital?
solution: Two spin states, so at most two.
hints: Each spin state holds one fermion.

prompt: Which exchange symmetry do identical bosons have?

options: Symmetric only if they are spatially separated.
why: the fermion rule
identical particles always have a definite symmetry
exchange symmetry does not depend on separation

solution: Bosons have symmetric total states.
hints: Bosons follow the opposite rule to fermions.

prompt: Two identical spinless fermions occupy the lowest possible levels of an infinite well. Find their total energy in units of $E_1$.
solution: They occupy $n=1$ and $n=2$, giving $E_1+4E_1=5E_1$.
hints: Pauli means each fermion needs its own level.

prompt: Two identical spinless bosons both occupy the ground state of an infinite well. Find their total energy in units of $E_1$.
solution: Bosons can share $n=1$, so $E=2E_1$.
hints: Bosons may share one state.

prompt: Two identical bosons occupy distinct orthonormal orbitals, with $f=\phi_a(x_1)\phi_b(x_2)$ and $g=\phi_b(x_1)\phi_a(x_2)$. Write the normalised symmetric spatial state in terms of $f$ and $g$.
solution: The symmetric combination is $(f+g)/\sqrt2$, which is normalised.
hints: Symmetrise over exchange of $x_1$ and $x_2$.

prompt: How many distinct two-particle states exist for two identical spin-one-half fermions in three spatial orbitals?
solution: Six single-particle states give $\binom62=15$ fermion pairs.
hints: Count pairs from six single-particle states.

prompt: Select all true statements about two identical electrons in the same spatial orbital.

options: Their spins must form a singlet

solution: A symmetric spatial part needs an antisymmetric spin part, which is the singlet. Two spin-up electrons would give a symmetric total state, which is forbidden.
hints: Work out which spin combination is antisymmetric.

prompt: Three identical spinless fermions occupy the three lowest levels of an infinite well. Find their total energy in units of $E_1$.
solution: They occupy $n=1,2,3$, giving $(1+4+9)E_1=14E_1$.
hints: Each fermion needs a distinct level.

prompt: A particle on the half-line has $\psi(x)=A\,x\,e^{-x/a}$ for $x\ge0$ and $\psi=0$ for $x<0$, with $a>0$ and $A$ real. Find the probability of finding it at $x>2a$.

why: used $e^{-x/a}$ instead of $e^{-2x/a}$ in $|\psi|^2$
dropped the factor $\tfrac12$ from normalisation
lost the $u^2$ term when integrating by parts
probability of $x<2a$ instead

hints: Normalise first, then integrate $|\psi|^2$ with the substitution $u=2x/a$.

prompt: A particle is in the $n=3$ stationary state of an infinite well $0<x<L$. Find the probability of finding it in $0<x<L/4$.

rubric.text: Evaluate the sine at $3\pi/2$ and combine

solution:
$\psi_3=\sqrt{2/L}\,\sin(3\pi x/L)$ (inf-well).
$P=\int_0^{L/4}\tfrac2L\sin^2\!\tfrac{3\pi x}{L}dx$ (born).
$=\tfrac1L\int_0^{L/4}\!\big(1-\cos\tfrac{6\pi x}{L}\big)dx=\tfrac14-\tfrac{1}{6\pi}\sin\tfrac{3\pi}{2}$.
$\sin(3\pi/2)=-1$, so $P=\tfrac14+\tfrac1{6\pi}\approx0.303$.
hints: Use the half-angle identity; the sine at $3\pi/2$ is $-1$, not $0$.

prompt: An electron ($m_e=9.11\times10^{-31}\ \mathrm{kg}$, $\hbar=1.05\times10^{-34}\ \mathrm{J\,s}$, $q=1.60\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm C$) has the stationary state $\psi=Ae^{-x^2/2b^2}$ with energy $E=\hbar^2/(2mb^2)$, where $b=0.50\ \mathrm{nm}$, in an even potential that is a pure parabola $V=\tfrac12m\omega^2x^2$. Find $\hbar\omega$ in eV.

rubric.text: Match to $\tfrac12m\omega^2x^2$ and convert to eV

solution:
$\psi''/\psi=x^2/b^4-1/b^2$ (tise).
$V=E+\tfrac{\hbar^2}{2m}\psi''/\psi=\dfrac{\hbar^2x^2}{2mb^4}$ (tise).
Compare with $\tfrac12m\omega^2x^2$: $\omega=\hbar/(mb^2)$ (qho).
$\hbar\omega=\hbar^2/(mb^2)=4.84\times10^{-20}\ \mathrm J\approx0.30\ \mathrm{eV}$.
hints: Insert $\psi$ into $-\tfrac{\hbar^2}{2m}\psi''+V\psi=E\psi$ and solve for $V$.

prompt: An electron ($m_e=9.11\times10^{-31}\ \mathrm{kg}$, $\hbar=1.05\times10^{-34}\ \mathrm{J\,s}$, $q=1.60\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm C$) sits in $V(x)=-\alpha\,\delta(x)$ with $\alpha=0.20\ \mathrm{eV\,nm}$. Its single bound state is $\psi\propto e^{-\kappa|x|}$. Find the rms position $\sqrt{\langle x^2\rangle}$ in nm.

rubric.text: Derivative jump at the delta gives $\kappa=m\alpha/\hbar^2$
Numbers: $\alpha$ in J m, then nm

solution:
Integrate the Schrodinger equation across $x=0$: $\Delta\psi'=-\tfrac{2m\alpha}{\hbar^2}\psi(0)$ (tise).
With $\psi'$ jumping by $-2\kappa\psi(0)$: $\kappa=m\alpha/\hbar^2$.
$|\psi|^2=\kappa e^{-2\kappa|x|}$; $\langle x^2\rangle=2\kappa\!\int_0^\infty x^2e^{-2\kappa x}dx=1/(2\kappa^2)$ (born).
$\alpha=3.2\times10^{-29}\ \mathrm{J\,m}$, $\kappa=2.64\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{m^{-1}}$.
$x_{rms}=1/(\sqrt2\kappa)\approx0.27\ \mathrm{nm}$.
hints: The jump in $\psi'$ across the delta fixes $\kappa$.

prompt: A particle is in the ground state of an infinite well $0<x<L$. The right wall is moved instantly to $x=2L$. Find the probability that the particle is then in the ground state of the enlarged well.

why: guessed from the width ratio
overlap amplitude, not squared
new ground state normalised with $2/L$ instead of $1/L$
dropped the $\sqrt2$ from the two normalisations

rubric.text: Sudden change: wavefunction unchanged, so probability is $|\langle\phi_1|\psi_1\rangle|^2$

solution:
Instant move leaves $\psi_1=\sqrt{2/L}\sin(\pi x/L)$ on $[0,L]$ (inf-well).
New ground state $\phi_1=\sqrt{1/L}\sin(\pi x/2L)$ on $[0,2L]$.
Overlap $=\tfrac{\sqrt2}{L}\int_0^L\sin\tfrac{\pi x}{L}\sin\tfrac{\pi x}{2L}dx$ (dirac).
Integral $=\tfrac12\big[\tfrac{2L}\pi+\tfrac{2L}{3\pi}\big]=\tfrac{4L}{3\pi}$.
Overlap $=\dfrac{4\sqrt2}{3\pi}$; probability $=\dfrac{32}{9\pi^2}\approx0.36$.
hints: The state does not change in a sudden move; project it onto the new ground state.

prompt: An electron ($m_e=9.11\times10^{-31}\ \mathrm{kg}$, $h=6.63\times10^{-34}\ \mathrm{J\,s}$, $c=3.00\times10^8\ \mathrm{m/s}$) in an infinite well absorbs a photon of wavelength $620\ \mathrm{nm}$ and goes from $n=2$ to $n=3$ exactly. Find the well width $L$ in nm.
solution:
$E_\gamma=hc/\lambda=3.21\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm J\approx2.0\ \mathrm{eV}$ (units).
$E_n=n^2h^2/(8mL^2)$, so $E_3-E_2=5E_1$ (inf-well).
$E_1=E_\gamma/5=6.42\times10^{-20}\ \mathrm J$.
$L=h/\sqrt{8mE_1}\approx9.7\times10^{-10}\ \mathrm m=0.97\ \mathrm{nm}$.
hints: Energy gap between $n=2$ and $n=3$ is $5E_1$.

prompt: Particles of energy $E=2V_0$ move in from $x<0$ where $V=0$ and meet a step $V=V_0$ for $x>0$. Find the transmission probability, defined by probability flux.

why: used the reflection amplitude, not its square, in $T=1-R$
squared the transmitted amplitude and forgot the flux factor $k_2/k_1$ (exceeds 1)
naive equal split
took $k_2=k_1/2$

rubric.text: Match $\psi,\psi'$ at the step to get $r=(k_1-k_2)/(k_1+k_2)$

solution:
$k_1\propto\sqrt{E}$, $k_2\propto\sqrt{E-V_0}$, so $k_2/k_1=1/\sqrt2$ (step-tunnel).
Continuity of $\psi$ and $\psi'$: $r=(k_1-k_2)/(k_1+k_2)=(\sqrt2-1)/(\sqrt2+1)=3-2\sqrt2$ (tise).
$R=r^2=17-12\sqrt2\approx0.029$.
$T=1-R=12\sqrt2-16\approx0.97$ (flux conservation).
hints: Match $\psi$ and $\psi'$; transmission is $1-R$.

prompt: An electron ($m_e=9.11\times10^{-31}\ \mathrm{kg}$, $\hbar=1.05\times10^{-34}\ \mathrm{J\,s}$, $q=1.60\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm C$) tunnels through a rectangular barrier whose top is $2.0\ \mathrm{eV}$ above its energy. In the thick-barrier limit $T\propto e^{-2\kappa a}$. By what factor does $T$ fall when the width $a$ goes from $0.20\ \mathrm{nm}$ to $0.40\ \mathrm{nm}$?
solution:
$\kappa=\sqrt{2m(V_0-E)}/\hbar$ with $V_0-E=3.2\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm J$ (step-tunnel).
$\kappa\approx7.27\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{m^{-1}}$.
Same prefactor, so $T_1/T_2=e^{2\kappa(0.20\ \mathrm{nm})}$ (scaling).
Exponent $=2.91$; factor $\approx18$.
hints: The prefactor cancels in the ratio; only the exponent difference matters.

prompt: In the oscillator ground state $\psi_0\propto e^{-\xi^2/2}$ with $\xi=x\sqrt{m\omega/\hbar}$, find the probability of finding the particle outside the classical turning points. Give the dimensionless number.
solution:
$E_0=\tfrac12\hbar\omega=\tfrac12 m\omega^2x_t^2$ gives $\xi_t=1$ (qho).
$|\psi_0|^2=\pi^{-1/2}e^{-\xi^2}$ (born).
$P=2\int_1^\infty\pi^{-1/2}e^{-\xi^2}d\xi=\mathrm{erfc}(1)$.
$P\approx0.157$.
hints: Find $\xi$ at which $E_0=V$; then integrate the Gaussian tails.

prompt: An oscillator is in $|\psi\rangle=(|0\rangle+|2\rangle)/\sqrt2$ with real standard $|n\rangle$ ($a|n\rangle=\sqrt n|n-1\rangle$). Find $\langle x^2\rangle$ in units of $\hbar/(m\omega)$.

why: incoherent mixture, cross term dropped
sign error on the cross term
cross term counted twice over
only $\langle2|x^2|2\rangle$

solution:
$x^2=\tfrac{\hbar}{2m\omega}(a^2+a^{\dagger2}+2a^\dagger a+1)$ (operators).
$\langle0|x^2|0\rangle=\tfrac12$, $\langle2|x^2|2\rangle=\tfrac52$ (qho).
$\langle0|x^2|2\rangle=\tfrac12\langle0|a^2|2\rangle=\tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}$ (dirac).
$\langle x^2\rangle=\tfrac12\big(\tfrac12+\tfrac52\big)+2\cdot\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac{\sqrt2}2=\tfrac{3+\sqrt2}{2}$.
hints: Interference between $|0\rangle$ and $|2\rangle$ enters through $a^2$ and $a^{\dagger2}$.

prompt: A particle with $H=p^2/2m+\lambda x^4$ ($\lambda>0$) is in a stationary state. Find $\langle T\rangle/\langle V\rangle$.

why: harmonic-oscillator result
dropped the factor 2 in $2\langle T\rangle=\langle xV'\rangle$
ratio inverted
inverted and dropped the 2

rubric.text: Stationary: zero, so $2\langle T\rangle=\langle xV'\rangle=4\langle V\rangle$

solution:
$d\langle xp\rangle/dt=\langle 2T-xV'\rangle$ (operators).
A stationary state has $d\langle A\rangle/dt=0$, so $2\langle T\rangle=\langle x\,dV/dx\rangle$ (hamiltonian).
$x\,dV/dx=4\lambda x^4=4V$.
$\langle T\rangle=2\langle V\rangle$; ratio $2$.
hints: Use the time derivative of $\langle xp\rangle$ in a stationary state.

prompt: For $H=p^2/2m+V(x)$ and ground state $|0\rangle$, expand $\langle0|[x,[x,H]]|0\rangle$ over energy eigenstates. For a harmonic oscillator only $|1\rangle$ has $\langle n|x|0\rangle\ne0$. Find $|\langle1|x|0\rangle|^2$.

why: missed the factor $\tfrac12$ in the sum rule
extra factor $\tfrac12$
factor 2 slip in the double commutator
gave the amplitude $|\langle1|x|0\rangle|$ shape, not its square

solution:
$[x,H]=i\hbar p/m$, so $[x,[x,H]]=(i\hbar/m)(i\hbar)=-\hbar^2/m$ (operators).
Insert $\sum|n\rangle\langle n|$: $\langle0|[x,[x,H]]|0\rangle=-2\sum_n(E_n-E_0)|\langle n|x|0\rangle|^2$ (dirac).
So $\sum_n(E_n-E_0)|x_{n0}|^2=\hbar^2/2m$.
Only $n=1$, gap $\hbar\omega$ (qho): $|x_{10}|^2=\dfrac{\hbar}{2m\omega}$.
hints: Expand the double commutator in a complete set; all $n\ne1$ drop out.

prompt: An electron ($m_e=9.11\times10^{-31}\ \mathrm{kg}$, $\hbar=1.05\times10^{-34}\ \mathrm{J\,s}$, $q=1.60\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm C$) has $\langle p\rangle=0$ and position spread $\Delta x=0.10\ \mathrm{nm}$. Using $\Delta x\,\Delta p\ge\hbar/2$, find the smallest possible $\langle p^2\rangle/2m$ in eV.
solution:
$\langle p\rangle=0$ gives $\langle p^2\rangle=(\Delta p)^2$ (uncertainty).
$\Delta p\ge\hbar/(2\Delta x)$.
$K_{min}=\hbar^2/(8m\,\Delta x^2)=1.51\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm J$ (estimate).
$\approx0.95\ \mathrm{eV}$.
hints: Remember the $\hbar/2$ bound, not $\hbar$.

prompt: A spin-$\tfrac12$ particle is in the eigenstate of $S_x$ with eigenvalue $+\hbar/2$. Find $\Delta S_y\,\Delta S_z$ in units of $\hbar^2$.

why: assumed an $S_x$ eigenstate has no spread in any component
used $\tfrac12\hbar\cdot\hbar/4$
forgot the $\tfrac12$ in the Robertson bound and took $\hbar^2/2$
squared an extra $\tfrac12$

solution:
$\langle S_y\rangle=\langle S_z\rangle=0$ in $|{+x}\rangle$ (spin-half).
$S_i^2=\hbar^2/4$, so $\Delta S_y=\Delta S_z=\hbar/2$.
Product $=\hbar^2/4$.
Bound: $\tfrac12\hbar|\langle S_x\rangle|=\hbar^2/4$ (uncertainty), so it saturates.
hints: Each component squared is $\hbar^2/4$; subtract the squared mean.

prompt: A system with orthonormal energy eigenstates $|1\rangle,|2\rangle,|3\rangle$ of energies $E,2E,3E$ is in $|\psi\rangle=(|1\rangle+i|2\rangle+2|3\rangle)/\sqrt6$. Find the energy spread $\Delta E=\sqrt{\langle H^2\rangle-\langle H\rangle^2}$.

why: quoted $\sqrt{\langle H^2\rangle}$
quoted $\langle H\rangle$
factor $\sqrt2$ slip in the variance
forgot the square root

solution:
$|c_n|^2=\tfrac16,\tfrac16,\tfrac23$ (born); the phase $i$ drops out.
$\langle H\rangle=\tfrac16(1)+\tfrac16(2)+\tfrac46(3)=\tfrac52$ in units of $E$ (dirac).
$\langle H^2\rangle=\tfrac16(1)+\tfrac16(4)+\tfrac46(9)=\tfrac{41}6$.
$\mathrm{Var}=\tfrac{41}6-\tfrac{25}4=\tfrac7{12}$; $\Delta E=\sqrt{7/12}\,E$.
hints: Use the squared amplitudes as weights for $E$ and $E^2$.

prompt: At $t=0$ an oscillator is in $(|0\rangle+|1\rangle)/\sqrt2$, with real standard $|n\rangle$ so $\langle0|x|1\rangle=+\sqrt{\hbar/2m\omega}$. Let $\ell=\sqrt{\hbar/m\omega}$ and period $T=2\pi/\omega$. Find $\langle x\rangle$ at $t=T/6$.

why: extra factor $\tfrac12$ in the cross term
the $t=0$ value
dropped $1/\sqrt2$ from $\langle0|x|1\rangle$ shape
used $\sin(\pi/3)$ for $\cos(\pi/3)$

solution:
$|\psi(t)\rangle=(|0\rangle+e^{-i\omega t}|1\rangle)/\sqrt2$ (time-evol).
$\langle x\rangle=2\cdot\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac{\ell}{\sqrt2}\cos\omega t=\tfrac{\ell}{\sqrt2}\cos\omega t$ (dirac).
At $t=T/6$, $\omega t=\pi/3$, $\cos=\tfrac12$.
$\langle x\rangle=\ell/(2\sqrt2)$.
hints: Only the relative phase $e^{-i\omega t}$ between $|0\rangle$ and $|1\rangle$ matters.

prompt: Spin-$\tfrac12$ particles prepared in $S_z=+\hbar/2$ pass first an analyser along $\hat n$, lying in the $xz$-plane at $60^\circ$ to $+z$, keeping the $+$ output. They then meet an analyser along $z$ that keeps the $-$ output. Find the probability that a particle entering the first analyser leaves the second.

why: second stage only
assumed the intermediate stage randomises (so $\tfrac12$) times $\cos^2$
used $\sin^2 30^\circ\cdot\tfrac12$
used $\cos^2 30^\circ$ twice

solution:
Angle between spin axes is $\theta$; overlap probability for same sign is $\cos^2(\theta/2)$ (spin-half).
Stage 1: $\cos^2 30^\circ=\tfrac34$.
Stage 2: $|{+n}\rangle\to|{-z}\rangle$ has $\sin^2 30^\circ=\tfrac14$ (born).
Product $=\tfrac3{16}$.
hints: Use half the angle between axes: $\cos^2(\theta/2)$ for the same sign, $\sin^2$ for opposite.

prompt: An electron ($g=2$, so the Larmor angular frequency is $\omega_L=qB/m_e$; $q=1.60\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm C$, $m_e=9.11\times10^{-31}\ \mathrm{kg}$) has spin along $+x$ at $t=0$ in $B=0.50\ \mathrm T$ along $z$. Find the first time at which $\langle S_x\rangle=-\hbar/2$, in ps.

rubric.text: Reversal of $\langle S_x\rangle$ requires a rotation of $\pi$

solution:
$\omega_L=qB/m=8.78\times10^{10}\ \mathrm{rad/s}$ (spin-half, lorentz).
$\langle\vec S\rangle$ precesses about $z$ at $\omega_L$.
$\langle S_x\rangle=\tfrac\hbar2\cos\omega_Lt$ reaches $-\hbar/2$ at $\omega_Lt=\pi$.
$t=\pi/\omega_L\approx3.6\times10^{-11}\ \mathrm s=36\ \mathrm{ps}$.
hints: A half turn of precession is needed, not a quarter turn.

prompt: A particle is in $|l=2,m=1\rangle$. Find $\langle L_x^2\rangle$ in units of $\hbar^2$.

why: used $l^2$ instead of $l(l+1)$
forgot the $\tfrac12$ symmetry split
took $L^2/2$, ignoring $L_z^2$
added $m^2$ instead of subtracting

rubric.text: Symmetry $\langle L_x^2\rangle=\langle L_y^2\rangle$ in an $L_z$ eigenstate

solution:
$\langle L^2\rangle=l(l+1)\hbar^2=6\hbar^2$ (ang-mom-qm).
$\langle L_z^2\rangle=m^2\hbar^2=\hbar^2$.
$\langle L_x^2\rangle=\langle L_y^2\rangle$ by rotation symmetry about $z$ (operators).
$\langle L_x^2\rangle=\tfrac12(6-1)\hbar^2=\tfrac52\hbar^2$.
hints: Split $L^2-L_z^2$ equally between $x$ and $y$.

prompt: A diatomic molecule is a rigid rotor with $I=1.45\times10^{-46}\ \mathrm{kg\,m^2}$ and $E_l=\hbar^2l(l+1)/2I$. Using $\hbar=1.05\times10^{-34}\ \mathrm{J\,s}$, $h=6.63\times10^{-34}\ \mathrm{J\,s}$ and $c=3.00\times10^8\ \mathrm{m/s}$, find the wavelength in mm of the photon emitted in the $l=2\to l=1$ transition.
solution:
$E_l=\hbar^2l(l+1)/2I$ gives $E_2=3\hbar^2/I$, $E_1=\hbar^2/I$ (ang-mom-qm).
$\Delta E=2\hbar^2/I=1.52\times10^{-22}\ \mathrm J$ (rot-dynamics).
$\lambda=hc/\Delta E=1.31\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm m$.
$\lambda\approx1.3\ \mathrm{mm}$.
hints: Use $l(l+1)$ for both levels before subtracting.

prompt: An electron ($m_e=9.11\times10^{-31}\ \mathrm{kg}$, $\hbar=1.05\times10^{-34}\ \mathrm{J\,s}$) in an infinite well of width $L=1.0\ \mathrm{nm}$ starts in $(\phi_1+\phi_2)/\sqrt2$. Find the period of the oscillation of $\langle x\rangle$ in fs.

rubric.text: Only the $\phi_1$--$\phi_2$ beat survives in $\langle x\rangle$

solution:
$\langle x\rangle$ contains the cross term $\propto\cos[(E_2-E_1)t/\hbar]$ (time-evol).
$E_n=n^2\pi^2\hbar^2/(2mL^2)$, so $E_2-E_1=3E_1$ (inf-well).
$T=2\pi\hbar/(3E_1)=4mL^2/(3\pi\hbar)$.
$T\approx3.7\times10^{-15}\ \mathrm s=3.7\ \mathrm{fs}$.
hints: The oscillation frequency is the energy gap over $\hbar$.

prompt: A free electron ($m_e=9.11\times10^{-31}\ \mathrm{kg}$, $\hbar=1.05\times10^{-34}\ \mathrm{J\,s}$) starts as a minimum-uncertainty Gaussian packet with $\Delta x_0=1.0\ \mathrm{nm}$. Its width obeys $\Delta x(t)=\Delta x_0\sqrt{1+(\hbar t/2m\Delta x_0^2)^2}$. Find the time in fs at which $\Delta x=2\Delta x_0$.
solution:
Doubling needs $1+u^2=4$ with $u=\hbar t/2m\Delta x_0^2$ (time-evol).
$u=\sqrt3$.
Spread comes from $\Delta p=\hbar/2\Delta x_0$ (uncertainty); scale $2m\Delta x_0^2/\hbar=1.74\times10^{-14}\ \mathrm s$.
$t=\sqrt3\times17.4\ \mathrm{fs}\approx30\ \mathrm{fs}$.
hints: Doubling means the square root equals 2, not that the bracket equals 2.

prompt: A two-level system has $H=\begin{pmatrix}E_0&A\\A&E_0\end{pmatrix}$ in the basis $(|1\rangle,|2\rangle)$ with $A=0.020\ \mathrm{eV}$. It starts in $|1\rangle$. Using $\hbar=1.05\times10^{-34}\ \mathrm{J\,s}$ and $q=1.60\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm C$, find the first time in fs at which the probability of $|2\rangle$ is $\tfrac12$.
solution:
Eigenstates $(|1\rangle\pm|2\rangle)/\sqrt2$, $E=E_0\pm A$ (two-level).
$|\psi(t)\rangle\propto\cos(At/\hbar)|1\rangle-i\sin(At/\hbar)|2\rangle$ (time-evol).
$P_2=\sin^2(At/\hbar)=\tfrac12$ gives $At/\hbar=\pi/4$.
$t=\pi\hbar/4A=2.58\times10^{-14}\ \mathrm s\approx26\ \mathrm{fs}$.
hints: Splitting between eigenvalues is $2A$, so the oscillation is $\sin^2(At/\hbar)$.

prompt: A two-level system has $H=\begin{pmatrix}0&\Delta\\\Delta&\varepsilon\end{pmatrix}$ with $\varepsilon=3\Delta$ and starts in the first basis state. Find the maximum probability of ever finding it in the second basis state.

why: probability of staying, not of transferring
used $\Delta^2/(\Delta^2+\varepsilon^2)$, missing the factor 4
dropped $4\Delta^2$ from the denominator
amplitude $2\Delta/\varepsilon$, not squared

solution:
$P_2(t)=\sin^22\theta\,\sin^2(\Omega t/2)$ with $\tan2\theta=2\Delta/\varepsilon$ (two-level).
$\sin^22\theta=\dfrac{4\Delta^2}{4\Delta^2+\varepsilon^2}$ (dirac).
The sine factor reaches 1 at some time, so $P_{max}=\sin^22\theta$.
$\varepsilon=3\Delta$: $P_{max}=4/13$.
hints: Maximum transfer equals $\sin^2$ of the mixing angle $2\theta$.

prompt: An infinite well of width $L=1.5\ \mathrm{nm}$ ($0<x<L$) gets the perturbation $H'=\alpha\,\delta(x-L/3)$ with $\alpha=0.60\ \mathrm{eV\,nm}$. Find the first-order energy shift of the $n=2$ state in eV.
solution:
$E^{(1)}=\langle\psi_2|H'|\psi_2\rangle$ (perturbation).
$=\alpha|\psi_2(L/3)|^2$ (inf-well).
$|\psi_2(L/3)|^2=\tfrac2L\sin^2(2\pi/3)=\tfrac2L\cdot\tfrac34$.
$E^{(1)}=0.60\times\tfrac{3}{2\times1.5}=0.60\ \mathrm{eV}$.
hints: A delta perturbation samples $|\psi|^2$ at one point.

prompt: An oscillator has the perturbation $H'=bx^4$. With $\ell^2=\hbar/(m\omega)$ and $x=\tfrac{\ell}{\sqrt2}(a+a^\dagger)$, find the first-order shift of the $n=1$ level in units of $b\ell^4$.

why: ground-state value (used $n=0$)
prefactor $\ell^4/16$ from $x=\tfrac\ell2(a+a^\dagger)$
prefactor $\ell^4/2$ from a dropped square
$\langle x^2\rangle^2$ factorisation

solution:
$E^{(1)}_n=b\langle n|x^4|n\rangle$ (perturbation).
$x^4=\tfrac{\ell^4}{4}(a+a^\dagger)^4$ (operators).
Keep terms with equal numbers of $a$ and $a^\dagger$: $\langle n|\cdot|n\rangle=6n^2+6n+3$ (qho).
$n=1$: $15$; $E^{(1)}=\tfrac{15}{4}b\ell^4$.
hints: Only terms with two $a$ and two $a^\dagger$ contribute; count them via $6n^2+6n+3$.

prompt: Use the trial function $\psi=e^{-\alpha x^2}$ to bound the ground-state energy of $H=p^2/2m+\lambda x^4$. Take $\langle p^2\rangle/2m=\hbar^2\alpha/2m$ and $\langle x^4\rangle=3/(16\alpha^2)$. The optimum $E$ equals $c\,(\hbar^4\lambda/m^2)^{1/3}$. Find $c$.

why: used $\langle x^4\rangle=\langle x^2\rangle^2$
used $\langle x^2\rangle=1/2\alpha$ error giving $\langle x^4\rangle=3/4\alpha^2$
set $\langle T\rangle=\langle V\rangle$ instead of minimising
doubled kinetic term and used $\langle x^4\rangle=1/16\alpha^2$

solution:
$E(\alpha)=\dfrac{\hbar^2\alpha}{2m}+\dfrac{3\lambda}{16\alpha^2}$ (variational).
$dE/d\alpha=0$: $\dfrac{\hbar^2}{2m}=\dfrac{3\lambda}{8\alpha^3}$, so $\alpha^3=\dfrac{3m\lambda}{4\hbar^2}$.
Then $\dfrac{3\lambda}{16\alpha^2}=\dfrac{\hbar^2\alpha}{4m}$ and $E=\dfrac{3\hbar^2\alpha}{4m}$ (tise).
$E=\tfrac34(\tfrac34)^{1/3}(\hbar^4\lambda/m^2)^{1/3}\approx0.68\,(\hbar^4\lambda/m^2)^{1/3}$.
hints: Minimise over $\alpha$; do not set $T=V$.

prompt: A particle moves in $V=F|x|$ with $F>0$. Using WKB with $\oint p\,dx=(n+\tfrac12)\,2\pi\hbar$ for $n=0,1,2,\dots$, find $E_2/E_0$.

why: oscillator scaling $E\propto n+\tfrac12$
inverted exponent
used $n+1$ in place of $n+\tfrac12$
infinite-well scaling $E\propto(n+\tfrac12)^2$

solution:
$\oint p\,dx=4\int_0^{E/F}\sqrt{2m(E-Fx)}\,dx=\dfrac{8\sqrt{2m}}{3F}E^{3/2}$ (variational/WKB).
Set equal to $(n+\tfrac12)2\pi\hbar$: $E\propto(n+\tfrac12)^{2/3}$ (tise).
$E_2/E_0=(2.5/0.5)^{2/3}=5^{2/3}$.
$\approx2.92$.
hints: Phase-space area scales as $E^{3/2}$ for a linear potential.

prompt: Five non-interacting electrons (spin-$\tfrac12$) fill an infinite well of width $L=1.0\ \mathrm{nm}$. The ground state occupies $n=1,1,2,2,3$. Find the lowest nonzero excitation energy of the system in eV (spin flips cost nothing and are ignored), using $m_e=9.11\times10^{-31}\ \mathrm{kg}$, $\hbar=1.05\times10^{-34}\ \mathrm{J\,s}$, $q=1.60\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm C$.

rubric.text: Pauli: at most two electrons per level

solution:
Pauli limits each $n$ to two electrons (identical).
Level $n=3$ has one electron, so it can accept one more.
Options: $2\to3$ costs $(9-4)E_1=5E_1$; $3\to4$ costs $7E_1$; $1\to3$ costs $8E_1$ (inf-well).
Lowest is $5E_1$ with $E_1=\pi^2\hbar^2/2mL^2=0.373\ \mathrm{eV}$; answer $1.87\ \mathrm{eV}$.
hints: A promotion needs an empty slot; level $n=3$ still has one.

prompt: Two identical spin-0 bosons in an infinite well $0<x<L$ occupy $\phi_1$ and $\phi_2$ in the symmetric state $[\phi_1(x_1)\phi_2(x_2)+\phi_2(x_1)\phi_1(x_2)]/\sqrt2$. Find the probability that both lie in $0<x<L/2$.

why: distinguishable-particle result, exchange term dropped
antisymmetric (fermion) sign
exchange overlap not squared
exchange term doubled

rubric.text: Each of $\phi_1,\phi_2$ has probability $\tfrac12$ in the left half

solution:
$P=\tfrac12\iint_{\text{left}}|\phi_1\phi_2'+\phi_2\phi_1'|^2$ expands to direct plus exchange (identical).
Direct: $P_1P_2=\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac12=\tfrac14$ (inf-well).
Exchange: $I=\tfrac2L\int_0^{L/2}\sin\tfrac{\pi x}{L}\sin\tfrac{2\pi x}{L}dx=\tfrac{4}{3\pi}$ (dirac).
Bosons add $I^2$: $P=\tfrac14+\tfrac{16}{9\pi^2}\approx0.43$.
hints: The symmetric state adds an exchange term $I^2$ to the product of single-particle probabilities.

prompt: State the energy of the hydrogen level with principal quantum number $n$.

why: drops the square on $n$
inverts the dependence on $n$
gives the wrong sign for a bound state

solution: Bound levels have $E_n=-13.6\ \mathrm{eV}/n^2$. They are negative and shrink in magnitude as $n$ grows.
hints: Bound states have negative energy that rises toward zero as $n$ grows.

prompt: Write the energy in eV of a photon emitted when a hydrogen electron falls from level $n$ to level $2$, for $n>2$, in terms of $n$. Use $13.6$ eV as the ground-state binding energy.
solution: $E=13.6\,(1/2^2-1/n^2)$ eV. The lower level sets the first term.
hints: The lower level is $n=2$, so its term is $1/2^2$.

prompt: How many electron states have principal quantum number $n$ in hydrogen, ignoring spin?

why: counts only the $l=0$ states
counts spin as well, but the prompt ignores spin
counts one $m_s$ value per $n$ and drops $l$

solution: For each $l=0,\dots,n-1$ there are $2l+1$ values of $m_l$. The sum is $n^2$.
hints: Add the $2l+1$ states for each allowed $l$.

prompt: A one-electron ion with nuclear charge $Z=2$ (He$^+$) sits in its $n=2$ level. Hydrogen's ground-state binding energy is $13.6$ eV, and binding energy scales as $Z^2/n^2$. Find the energy in eV needed to remove the electron from this level.
solution: The factor is $Z^2/n^2=4/4=1$, so the energy is $13.6$ eV.
hints: Scale the hydrogen value by $Z^2$ and by $1/n^2$.

prompt: Find the wavelength in nm of the Balmer-alpha line, from $n=3$ to $n=2$. Use $h=6.63\times10^{-34}$ J s, $c=3.00\times10^{8}$ m/s, $q=1.60\times10^{-19}$ C, and ground-state binding energy $13.6$ eV.
hints: Get the photon energy first, then use $\lambda=hc/E$.

prompt: A hydrogen atom drops from $n=4$ to $n=2$. Find the photon energy in eV, using $13.6$ eV as the ground-state binding energy.
hints: Use the lower level as $n_f$ in the $1/n_f^2$ term.

prompt: In hydrogen, the Bohr radius of the $n=1$ orbit is $53$ pm. Find the radius in pm of the $n=2$ orbit of He$^+$, which has nuclear charge $Z=2$.
solution: The radius scales as $n^2/Z$, so $r=53\cdot4/2=106$ pm.
hints: A larger nuclear charge pulls the orbit inward.

prompt: Write the energy in eV of the photon emitted when a hydrogen electron falls from level $n$ to level $m$, with $n>m$, in terms of $n$ and $m$. Use $13.6$ eV as the ground-state binding energy.
solution: $E=13.6\,(1/m^2-1/n^2)$ eV, from the level energies $-13.6/k^2$.
hints: Subtract the upper level's energy magnitude from the lower one's.

prompt: Select all sets of quantum numbers $(n,\,l,\,m_l)$ allowed for an electron in hydrogen.
solution: $l$ runs from $0$ to $n-1$ and $|m_l|\le l$. $(3,3,0)$ needs $l\le2$, and $(3,1,2)$ needs $|m_l|\le1$.
hints: Check the range of $l$ and then the range of $m_l$.

prompt: State the allowed values of total angular momentum $j$ for an electron with orbital quantum number $l\ge1$ and spin $s=\tfrac12$.

why: drops the spin contribution
uses integer steps, which a half-integer spin cannot give
keeps only the spin and drops the orbital motion

solution: Spin $\tfrac12$ adds to $l$ to give $j=l+\tfrac12$ or $l-\tfrac12$, two fine-structure levels for $l\ge1$.
hints: Spin adds or subtracts a half-integer.

prompt: How many distinct values of $j$ does a $d$ electron ($l=2$) have? Enter the integer.
solution: $j=\tfrac52$ and $j=\tfrac32$, so two values.
hints: Use $j=l\pm\tfrac12$.

prompt: Which two angular momenta does the hyperfine interaction couple?

options: Orbit $L$ and spin $S$ of one electron
Nuclear spin $I$ and total electron angular momentum $J$
The spins of two different electrons
why: that coupling gives fine structure, not hyperfine structure
that is exchange physics, not hyperfine structure
omits the electron spin that the hyperfine term needs

solution: The nuclear magnetic moment interacts with the electron's total $\vec J$. This splits each fine level into $F=I+J,\dots,|I-J|$.
hints: The nucleus carries a spin of its own.

prompt: An atom has nuclear spin $I=\tfrac32$ and electron total angular momentum $J=\tfrac32$. How many distinct hyperfine levels $F$ does its ground state have? Enter the integer.
solution: $F$ runs from $|I-J|=0$ to $I+J=3$ in integer steps: $0,1,2,3$. That is four levels.
hints: List $F$ from $|I-J|$ up to $I+J$.

prompt: The hydrogen 21 cm line comes from a hyperfine splitting of $5.87\ \mu\mathrm{eV}$. Find its wavelength in cm. Use $h=6.63\times10^{-34}$ J s, $c=3.00\times10^{8}$ m/s, $q=1.60\times10^{-19}$ C.
solution: $\lambda=hc/\Delta E$ with $\Delta E=5.87\times10^{-6}\times1.60\times10^{-19}$ J, giving $0.212$ m $=21.2$ cm.
hints: Convert the energy to joules before using $hc/\Delta E$.

prompt: Hyperfine levels obey the Landé interval rule: the energy gap between $F$ and $F-1$ is $AF$. With $A=2.0\ \mu\mathrm{eV}$, find the gap between $F=3$ and $F=2$ in $\mu$eV.
solution: The gap uses the upper level's $F$: $A\cdot3=6.0\ \mu$eV.
hints: The rule multiplies $A$ by the upper $F$.

prompt: In hydrogen's $n=2$ level, which fine-structure level lies higher in energy, $2p_{1/2}$ or $2p_{3/2}$?

options: They are degenerate, since spin-orbit coupling vanishes in hydrogen
$2p_{3/2}$ lies lower, since larger $j$ means more binding
why: reverses the sign of the spin-orbit energy
drops the spin-orbit term that splits the level
gets the order backwards with a false heuristic

solution: The spin-orbit energy is positive for $j=l+\tfrac12$, so $2p_{3/2}$ lies above $2p_{1/2}$.
hints: Compare $\vec L\cdot\vec S$ for each value of $j$.

prompt: The spin-orbit shift is $A\,\vec L\cdot\vec S$, with $\vec L\cdot\vec S=\tfrac12[j(j+1)-l(l+1)-s(s+1)]$. Write the shift $\Delta E$ in terms of $A$, $j$ and $l$, with $s=\tfrac12$.
solution: With $s=\tfrac12$, $s(s+1)=\tfrac34$, so $\Delta E=\tfrac{A}{2}[j(j+1)-l(l+1)-\tfrac34]$.
hints: Substitute $s=\tfrac12$ into the bracket first.

prompt: For an atom with nuclear spin $I=1$ and electron $J=\tfrac12$, select all allowed values of the total $F$.
solution: $F$ runs from $|I-J|=\tfrac12$ to $I+J=\tfrac32$ in integer steps. So $F=\tfrac12$ and $F=\tfrac32$ are the only values.
hints: Step from $|I-J|$ to $I+J$ in integer steps.

prompt: State the Zeeman energy shift of a level with Landé factor $g_J$ and projection $m_J$ in a magnetic field $B$.

why: drops the Landé factor
drops the projection, so every level shifts equally
squares the projection, which loses its sign

solution: The shift is $\Delta E=g_Jm_J\mu_BB$. It is linear in $m_J$, so the sign of $m_J$ sets the direction.
hints: Start from the magnetic moment dotted into the field.

prompt: Is the Stark shift of the hydrogen ground state ($n=1$) linear or quadratic in the electric field?

options: Linear in $E$, because the ground state has a permanent dipole
Quadratic in $E$, because the field induces a dipole
Zero, because the level is not degenerate
Linear in $E$, with a sign set by $m_l$
why: assumes a permanent dipole, which exists only in degenerate-pair states
assumes a non-degenerate level cannot shift at all, but second order still acts
takes the linear rule, which needs a degenerate pair, and adds a sign from $m_l$

solution: The ground state has no degenerate partner, so the first-order shift vanishes and the shift is quadratic in $E$.
hints: Linear Stark splitting needs a degenerate pair of opposite parity.

prompt: Write the Zeeman energy shift $\Delta E$ in terms of the Bohr magneton $\mu_B$ (muB), the Landé factor $g$, the projection $m$ and the field $B$.
solution: $\Delta E=g\,m\,\mu_B B$.
hints: Multiply the three factors.

prompt: A free electron ($g=2$) sits in a field of $0.50$ T. Find the energy difference between its $m_s=+\tfrac12$ and $m_s=-\tfrac12$ states in $\mu$eV. Use $\mu_B=57.9\ \mu$eV/T.
solution: $\Delta E=g\mu_B B=2\times57.9\times0.50=57.9\ \mu$eV, since $m_s$ changes by $1$.
hints: The two projections differ by one unit.

prompt: Find the Landé factor $g_J$ for a level with $L=1$, $S=\tfrac12$, $J=\tfrac12$. Use $g_s=2$ and give a decimal.
hints: Compute $J(J+1)$, $S(S+1)$ and $L(L+1)$ first.

prompt: A level with $g_J=\tfrac23$ and $m_J=-\tfrac12$ sits in a field of $1.0$ T. Using $\mu_B=57.9\ \mu$eV/T, find its Zeeman shift in $\mu$eV.
solution: $\Delta E=g_Jm_J\mu_BB=\tfrac23\cdot(-\tfrac12)\cdot57.9\cdot1.0=-19.3\ \mu$eV.
hints: The sign of $m_J$ carries through to the shift.

prompt: A $^2P_{3/2}$ level ($J=\tfrac32$) is placed in a weak field. How many $m_J$ sublevels appear?

why: counts only the two extremes $m_J=\pm\tfrac32$
uses $2L+1$ from the orbital motion, not $2J+1$
multiplies $(2L+1)(2S+1)$, ignoring that $J$ fixes the sublevels

solution: A level with total $J$ has $2J+1$ sublevels, here $2(\tfrac32)+1=4$.
hints: Count $m_J$ from $-J$ to $+J$.

prompt: A level has total $j$ and Landé factor $g$. Write the energy difference between its $m_J=+j$ and $m_J=-j$ sublevels in a field $B$, in terms of $g$, $j$, $\mu_B$ (muB) and $B$.
solution: $\Delta E=g\mu_B B\,[\,j-(-j)\,]=2gj\mu_B B$.
hints: The two projections are $+j$ and $-j$.

prompt: Select all true statements about the normal Zeeman effect.

options: It splits a spin-zero line into three components
Adjacent components are separated by $\mu_B B$
The spacing grows with the principal quantum number $n$
It appears only in weak fields where spin-orbit coupling dominates

solution: Normal Zeeman has $g=1$, so a singlet line splits into three by $\Delta m_l=0,\pm1$, spaced $\mu_B B$. The weak-field spin-orbit case is anomalous.
hints: Normal Zeeman has $g=1$.

prompt: State the electric-dipole selection rule for the orbital quantum number $l$ of an atomic transition.

why: treats $l$ as conserved, which a dipole photon does not allow
is the electric quadrupole rule, not the dipole rule
drops the rule, but dipole transitions are restricted

solution: The photon carries one unit of angular momentum, so electric-dipole transitions obey $\Delta l=\pm1$.
hints: A dipole photon has spin 1.

prompt: State the electric-dipole rule on total angular momentum $j$ for a transition from $j_i$ to $j_f$.

why: forbids the $\Delta j=\pm1$ transitions
is the quadrupole rule
ignores the rule

solution: The photon carries $j=1$, so $|\Delta j|\le1$, and the $0\to0$ transition is forbidden.
hints: The photon adds at most one unit of $j$.

prompt: The Lyman series of hydrogen ends on which lower level $n_f$? Enter the integer.
solution: Lyman lines end at $n_f=1$; Balmer at $2$; Paschen at $3$.
hints: Lyman is the ultraviolet series.

prompt: Find the wavelength in nm of the allowed $3p\to1s$ transition (Lyman-$\beta$). Use $h=6.63\times10^{-34}$ J s, $c=3.00\times10^{8}$ m/s, $q=1.60\times10^{-19}$ C, and ground-state binding energy $13.6$ eV.
solution: $E=13.6\,(1-\tfrac19)=12.09$ eV, so $\lambda=hc/E\approx103$ nm.
hints: Lyman lines all end at $n=1$.

prompt: Select all transitions that are electric-dipole allowed.
solution: $2s\to1s$ and $3s\to2s$ have $\Delta l=0$, so they are forbidden. $2p\to1s$ and $3d\to2p$ have $\Delta l=-1$, so they are allowed.
hints: Check $\Delta l$ for each transition.
